We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

Whether it’s a dress, high heels, or any other style, the key is that it feels right for you and helps you project the energy you want to share with the world. If a particular heel height or dress length feels too tight, consider a slightly different cut or a supportive shoe insert. - **Body positivity**: Remember that confidence isn’t tied to a single style. It’s about how you feel inside. If you ever want to experiment, try different silhouettes or colors that make you feel good—no one rule applies to everyone. - **Social context**: Sometimes the setting can influence how you feel. If you’re heading to a formal event, a dress and heels might feel natural. For a casual outing, you could still keep the confidence boost by pairing a dress with flats or sneakers that match your vibe. Ultimately, the best outfit is the one that makes you feel like the best version of yourself. If a dress and high heels are your go‑to confidence boosters, own that choice and wear it proudly. And if you ever want to mix things up or explore new styles, feel free to experiment—confidence can be a fluid, evolving thing.
